items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we wish to factor the expression

Content:
[MATH: (8x+3){\color{blue}{(4-x)}} + {\color{red}{(x-4)}}(5x-7)]

Content:
At first glance, it seems as though there are no common factors.

Content:
However, upon closer inspection, we notice that

Content:
- the first term contains a factor of [MATH: {\color{blue}{(4-x)}},] and
- the second term contains a factor of [MATH: {\color{red}{(x-4)}}.]

Content:
These factors differ only by their sign:
[MATH: {\color{red}{(x-4)}} = -{\color{blue}{(4-x)}}.]

Content:
So, we first make the factors the same by factoring out [MATH: -1] in the second term, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (8x+3){\color{blue}{(4-x)}} - {\color{blue}{(4-x)}}(5x-7)]

Content:
Notice that the plus [MATH: (+)] symbol in front of the second term of our original expression has flipped to a minus symbol [MATH: (-).]

Content:
Now that our terms contain a common factor, we can factor the expression. This gives
[MATH: {\color{blue}{(4-x)}}\left[(8x+3) - (5x-7)\right].]

Content:
Finally, we simplify the expression inside the square brackets:
[MATH: (8x+3) - (5x-7) = 3x + 10]

Content:
So, our fully factored form is
[MATH: (4-x)(3x+10).]

sections.normalized_html: Factor the following expression: [MATH: (4y+1)(8y-7) - (7-8y)(6y-5)]
sections.readable_text:
Factor the following expression:
[MATH: (4y+1)(8y-7) - (7-8y)(6y-5)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We're asked to factor the expression [MATH: (4y+1)(8y-7) - (7-8y)(6y-5).]

Notice that

  • the first term in this expression contains a factor of [MATH: (8y-7),] and

  • the second term contains a factor of [MATH: (7-8y).]

These factors differ only by the sign: [MATH: 7-8y = -(8y-7).]

So, we first make the factors the same by factoring out [MATH: -1] in the second term: [MATH: (4y+1)(8y-7) + (8y-7)(6y-5)]

Now, we can factor the expression as follows: [MATH: (8y-7)\left[(4y+1) + (6y-5)\right]]

Finally, we simplify the expression inside the square brackets: [MATH: (4y+1) + (6y-5) = 10y - 4]

So the factored form is [MATH: (8y-7)(10y-4).]

sections.normalized_html: Factor the following expression: [MATH: (z-12)(z+3) + 4(12-z)^2]
sections.readable_text:
Factor the following expression:
[MATH: (z-12)(z+3) + 4(12-z)^2]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We're asked to factor the expression [MATH: (z-12)(z+3) + 4(12-z)^2.]

Notice that

  • the first term in this expression contains a factor of [MATH: (z-12),] and

  • the second term contains a factor of [MATH: (12-z).]

These factors differ only by the sign: [MATH: 12-z = -(z-12)]

However, the squaring eliminates the minus sign: [MATH: (12-z)^2 = (z-12)^2]

So, we can simply rewrite the second term: [MATH: (z-12)(z+3) + 4(z-12)^2]

Now, we can factor the expression as follows:

[MATH: (z-12)\left[(z+3) + 4(z-12)\right]]

Finally, we simplify the expression inside the square brackets. This gives [MATH: (z − 12)[(z + 3) + 4(z − 12)]|=; (z − 12)[z + 3 + 4z − 48]|=; (z − 12)(5z − 45).]

We're asked to factor the expression [MATH: (2a-7)^3(a+2) + (3a+4)(7-2a)^2.]

Notice that

  • the first term in this expression contains a factor of [MATH: (2a-7)^2,] and

  • the second term contains a factor of [MATH: (7-2a)^2.]

These factors differ only by the sign: [MATH: 7-2a = -(2a-7)]

However, the squaring eliminates the minus sign: [MATH: (7-2a)^2 = (2a-7)^2]

So, we can simply rewrite the second term: [MATH: (2a-7)^3(a+2) + (3a+4)(2a-7)^2]

Now, we can factor the expression as follows: [MATH: (2a-7)^2 \left[(2a-7)(a+2) + (3a+4)\right]]

Finally, we simplify the expression inside the square brackets. This gives [MATH: (2a − 7)^{2}[(2a − 7)(a + 2) + (3a + 4)]|=; (2a − 7)^{2}[2a^{2} + 4a − 7a − 14 + 3a + 4]|=; (2a − 7)^{2}(2a^{2} − 10)_(⏟)_(g(a)).]

Therefore, we have [MATH: g(a) = 2a^2 - 10.]
